pages.name: Fifty readings
pages.text: Each reading starts at the true value, 27.00 V, drawn dashed. Twelve pegs nudge it left or right on the way down. The nudges scatter the readings with a standard deviation of 0.04 V. That is the random error. Fifty readings rise into a swarm round 27.00 V. Most land within about 0.08 V either side. So a single reading could be any one of these beads.

pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings fall from a hopper over the true value, 27.00 volts, through a field of pegs. They land on a beam and rise into a swarm, each bead coloured by how far it sits from the mean. The beam balances at their mean, marked with its value. pages.name: Average a few
pages.text: Here each bead is the mean of four readings. The random errors of the readings in a bead point different ways, so they partly cancel. With two a bead the swarm narrows to about seven tenths of its width. With four it is half as wide. It still centres on 27.00 V. So the spread of a mean is the spread of one reading divided by the square root of how many are averaged.

pages.name: Mean of four
pages.task: One reading's random error is 0.04 V. Each bead is the mean of four readings. What is the beads' standard deviation?
pages.why: Four readings a bead divide the spread by √4, which is 2. So 0.04 V ÷ 2 = 0.02 V. The bracket shows 1 SD each side of the mean.

pages.name: The result
pages.text: Back to one reading a bead. The bracket over the swarm is the result. It is the mean of all fifty, ± its [[uncertainty]]. By the square-root rule, that mean spreads 0.04 ÷ √50. Twice a spread either side catches about 95%. So the result reaches 2 × 0.04 ÷ √50 either side. With √50 about 7.07, that is about 0.011 V. Give the value to the same decimal place: 27.001 ± 0.011 V. The wide bracket under the beam shows where most single readings land.

pages.name: Read the rating
pages.task: A meter rated ±(1% + 3 digits) shows 50.0 V. It reads to 0.1 V. Where could the true voltage be?
pages.why: 1% of 50.0 V is 0.5 V. Three digits are three steps of 0.1 V, so 0.3 V. Together that is 0.8 V either side. So the true voltage could be anywhere from 49.2 V to 50.8 V.

pages.name: Reads high
pages.text: Here the meter reads 0.02 V high, and each bead is the mean of four readings. The shaded window is an example meter's accuracy, 0.047 V either side of 27.00 V. A meter within its rating can centre anywhere inside it. The whole swarm has shifted across. Averaging tightened it round 27.02 V, where the meter centres. The result, 27.020 ± 0.006 V, misses the dashed true value. The offset lands on every reading, so it lands on their mean too. That is a [[systematic error]].

pages.task: This meter reads 0.03 V high. You make each bead the mean of four readings instead of one. Where does the result centre now?
pages.answer: Near 27.03 V, with a narrower bracket
pages.why: Averaging four readings halves the random scatter, so the bracket narrows. But the 0.03 V offset is in every reading, so it is in their mean too. The result still centres near 27.03 V.

pages.name: Against a limit
pages.text: With four readings a bead, a dashed example upper limit sits at 27.02 V. Here the meter reads 0.02 V high, and the result overlaps the limit. From the readings alone, the true value could be either side. So it shows neither a pass nor a fail. At 0 and 0.01 V high the result sits below the limit. At 0.03 V it sits above, so the readings say fail. Yet the true value is still 27.00 V. A real bracket must also take in the meter's accuracy.

pages.task: A result is 0.82 ± 0.03 Ω at 95%. The example maximum is 0.84 Ω. What does it show?
pages.answer: Neither a pass nor a fail
pages.why: The bracket runs from 0.82 − 0.03 = 0.79 Ω to 0.82 + 0.03 = 0.85 Ω. It overlaps the 0.84 Ω maximum. So the true value could be either side, and the result shows neither a pass nor a fail. A real bracket must also take in the meter's accuracy.
